extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical mechanics (advanced undergraduate/graduate level) and readers of a mechanics textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical mechanics principles: the conservation of the centre of gravity, the law of conservation of areas (mass-areas/mass-sector law), and the laws of impact with illustrative examples and experimental analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a system can acquire no acceleration without the action of external forces; just as a single mass cannot accelerate without external force, a system's centre of gravity cannot accelerate without external forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: an animal moving parts of its body in free space cannot change the position of its overall centre of gravity; a vehicle on low-friction rails loaded with stones will move oppositely when stones are cast out so that the system centre of gravity remains fixed; when internal parts become rigidly connected the opposite momenta are destroyed and overall motion vanishes. Use this principle to analyse recoil, internal redistributions of mass, and whether system motions require external supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Momentum-conservation explanation of recoil (cannon example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a projectile of mass m is thrown from a cannon of mass M with projectile velocity v, the cannon receives recoil velocity V such that, allowing for signs, M V + m v = 0, giving V = - (m/M) v (for opposite signs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains recoil magnitude: for equal projectile velocities recoil is less when cannon mass is greater. If the work done by the powder is A, energies satisfy M V^2/2 + m v^2/2 = A; neglecting powder mass gives formulae for velocities. If mass were sucked in instead of expelled, recoil would be in the opposite direction but may be unobservable if the sucked-in mass quickly comes to rest relative to cannon (no visible recoil once rigid connection formed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of areas (mass-areas law)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a system of masses, the sum of the products of the areas described by radii (to any chosen point) into the respective masses is unaltered by internal forces — i.e. the algebraic sum of mass×area (mass-areas) is conserved under internal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction: for two mutually acting masses m and m' the areas described in opposite senses multiply with masses to sum zero; extend to several masses and projections on any plane. This law applies to free systems and remains valid if external forces act whose lines of action pass through the chosen point O. Use radii vectors and signed areas; practical use includes analysis of mutual actions, rotating systems, and sector-law type problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-areas increase law for free masses
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single mass moving uniformly with no forces is referenced from any point O, the area described by its radius vector increases proportionally to time; for several such masses the sum of mass-areas increases proportionally to time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When external accelerative forces (assumed constant over small intervals) act, the sum of mass-areas increases according to a quadratic/time-law depending on accelerative force, initial velocity and position — internal forces do not affect this increase. Apply for short-time approximations where accelerative forces may be considered constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of area-law to rigid bodies (relation to moment of inertia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A free rigid body is a system whose parts are held in relative position by internal forces; the law of areas applies. For uniform rotation about an axis through the centre of gravity, the sum of mass-areas produced in unit time equals one-half the angular velocity times the moment of inertia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If m is a mass element at distance r and angular velocity ω, contribution per unit time = (ω/2) * 2 m r^2 = (ω/2) * (2 m r^2); overall this equals (moment_of_inertia) * (ω/2). Only external forces can alter this product. Use this to connect the area-law to angular momentum concepts and for rotating rigid body analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite rotation from internal forces in free systems
rubrics_metrics.description: If two rigid bodies K and K' are connected and internal forces set K rotating relative to K', K' will be set rotating in the opposite direction so that the total sum of mass-areas is conserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical illustrations: electromotor flywheel causing opposite rotation of motor body (when free); reaction-wheels; torque balancing in coupled rotating parts. Use to predict counter-rotation and design counterweights/balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensating oscillations by balancing masses (locomotive example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oscillatory motion of internal heavy masses (e.g., piston-rods) imparts opposite oscillation to the locomotive body; to eliminate this the moving masses must be compensated by contrary-moving masses so that the system's centre of gravity remains fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineering solution: affix balance weights to driving wheels so the centre of gravity of the whole remains stationary and the body does not oscillate. Use for design of wheels and counterbalances to smooth vehicle motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electromotor/flywheel balance illustration and friction effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An iron core moving internally produces an opposite displacement of the motor body if the motor rests on lightly movable wheels; affixing a balancing weight to the flywheel that moves contrary to the core can make sideward motion vanish. When current is interrupted frictional forces cause a sequence of relative motions and eventual reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how internal electromagnetic forces generate compensating motions; friction is an external force that breaks perfect freedom — after current interruption, frictional damping can cause the parts to assume relative rest and then exhibit net rotation in the wheel's original direction. Use to understand practical deviations from ideal conservation due to friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre-of-gravity principle applied to explosions
rubrics_metrics.description: After a bursting bomb, making allowance for air resistance and obstacles, the centre of gravity of the fragments continues to describe the parabolic path of the original projection (i.e., centre-of-gravity motion conserved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to determine overall trajectory of fragment cloud and to separate external-resistance effects from internal fragmentation dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction-wheel and jet asymmetry (blowing vs sucking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emitting air or gas from a reaction-wheel produces rotation in the opposite direction to the jet; sucking air in generally does not produce the opposite rotation because sucked air must be brought to relative rest with the wheel and so produces no compensating reactive rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermittent operation (alternately blowing and sucking equal quantities) can still produce net rotation in the blowing direction if the sucked-in air participates in the wheel's motion or if external flow patterns differ. Demonstrations: perforated cylinder turns differently when blown into versus sucked upon; attach an elastic ball to alternate and observe continued rotation. Apply when designing reaction propulsion and interpreting experimental asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid-stream in curved tube impulse and timing effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A tube that carries liquid along a curved circular path will experience a turning impulse while the fluid is in that path; the impulse ceases when the fluid reaches a point where it must join the further tube section and assume its motion, so a continuous stream soon stops imparting net rotation, whereas an interrupted stream can impart impulses producing rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between steady and intermittent flow when predicting rotational impulses on conduit systems. Use conservation of areas/mass-areas and momentum-transfer timing to predict net motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of angular velocity with changing moment of inertia (conservation implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body having moment of inertia Θ rotates with angular velocity ω and internal forces change the moment of inertia to Θ', then ω' = ω (Θ/Θ') — a decrease of moment of inertia produces a corresponding increase in angular velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications: pumping down fluid in a funnel causing decreased moment of inertia and increased angular velocity, creating strong eddies. Use as an alternative demonstration of Earth's rotation or for practical rotating-fluid devices; note friction and other external torques may alter the ideal result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation principles as expressions of action and reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre-of-gravity and law-of-areas principles are convenient modes of expressing the general property of reaction: to an acceleration cp of mass m corresponds a contrary acceleration cp' of m' such that m cp + m' cp' = 0; centre-of-gravity addresses parallel coordinates, area-law addresses polar coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret both principles as generalised statements of inertia: a system cannot change its mean motion (translation or rotation) without interaction with an external system. Use this conceptual link when teaching or reasoning about invariants and the physical meaning of conservation laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of impact: impulse (momentum) concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact is best characterised by the impulse or quantity of motion m v (momentum); instantaneous impacts impart small velocities which nonetheless produce motion against large static pressures — the force of percussion (impulse) is essentially different in dimension and nature from pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galileo's insight: impulse (momentum) has different dimensions from pressure; instantaneous impact cannot be counteracted by statical pressure arguments. Use m v as the fundamental quantity in impact problems, and be cautious converting to pressure without accounting for time (momentum per unit time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Galileo's falling-jet experiment decomposition (three factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: When fluid flows from an upper vessel I into a lower vessel II through a basal orifice, three pressure-variation factors act: (i) loss of weight due to the jet suspended in the air, (ii) upward reaction pressure exerted on vessel I by the effluent jet (momentum imparted per unit time), and (iii) pressure increase on vessel II due to jet impact on its bottom. These factors exactly compensate in steady operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical expressions provided: factor (i) = a v (s/g) * v ? (weight of jet in air), factor (ii) relates to momentum per unit time (mass flux × velocity), factor (iii) = mass_flux × w (velocity at surface); the total variation sums to zero in steady-state, explaining Galileo's observed negligible net depression. Use this decomposition to analyse jet impingement, reaction forces and experimental design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pressure and momentum (dimensions and measurability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure (force per area) and impulse/momentum (m v) are quantities of different dimensions; continuous fluid jets allow measurement of impact by comparing momentum destroyed per second with pressure (homogeneous quantities per second), but instantaneous impacts cannot be measured by pressure alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating dynamic impacts as statical pressure effects; in dynamical cases velocity is generated over time by inter-particle pressures, and correct evaluation requires momentum/impulse accounting (mv = p·t). Use momentum per unit time for continuous jets to compute equivalent steady pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of impact treatments (historical: elastic vs inelastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early systematic treatments separated elastic and inelastic impact laws: Wallis treated inelastic impact, Wren and Huygens treated elastic impact; experiments supported Huygens' theorems and were later used by Newton and Mariotte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solving impact problems, identify whether collisions are elastic or inelastic and apply the corresponding conservation relations (momentum always; kinetic energy conserved in elastic collisions). Consult historical approaches for experimental setups (percussion-machine) to validate theoretical results.
